Models tend to bias toward stronger or more informative modalities, which underutilizes others and de- grades overall performance [19, 20]. Incomplete Multi-modal Learning Incomplete multi-modal learning targets scenarios where some modalities are missing because of hardware limits, cost, or privacy. Existing methods 3 fall roughly into two categories. Reconstruction-based methods impute miss- ing data through generative models or cross-modal transfer prior to fusion [8– 10, 12, 25]. Examples include Transformer-based patch reconstruction [9] and encoder–decoder completion networks [10]. Analysis-based methods avoid ex- plicit reconstruction and instead focus on filtering irrelevant components or extracting shared features for fusion [11, 13, 26, 27]. Representative techniques include substituting missing-modality inputs with shared features [11] or disen- tangling common and modality-specific features to improve fusion [13]. A common limitation across these works is the assumption of random miss- ingness. They are not designed for the more challenging case of imbalanced missing rates, where systematic absence of particular modalities induces persis- tent bias and harms representation learning. 2.3. Discussion: Computational Considerations and Practical Trade- offs The Shapley value calculation is justified by its unique benefits. Unlike heuristic approaches that rely solely on missing rates or importance measures, theShapleyvalueaccountsforbothindividualmodalitycontributionsandtheir interactions within different coalitions. This comprehensive method enables more precise allocation of learning resources, particularly for underrepresented modalities that may otherwise be overlooked. However, despite its advantages, the Shapley value introduces both computational and memory overhead, as shown in Tab. 8. While the memory overhead increases from 1425 MB to 1589 MB, it is modest compared to the substantial increase in processing time. The exact Shapley value computation increases processing time by approximately 12× compared to baseline implementations. This is due to the exponential complexity (O(2M)) of evaluating all possible modality subsets, which becomes prohibitive as the number of modalities increases. 21 WeconsidertoemploytheMonteCarlosamplingstrategy,reducingthecom- plexitytoO(K·M)byconsideringK randompermutationsofmodalityjoining orders for each sample. In our experiments, K =100. The reasons are: i) pro- viding a consistent and stable valuation across diverse modality subsets arising from different missing patterns; ii) reducing estimation variance by oversam- pling, ensuring that Shapley values yield smooth and reliable gradient signals; iii) optimizing efficiency by avoiding recomputation for identical sampling out- comes, instead using a weighted summation of the results. This approximation significantlyreducescomputationaldemandswhilemaintainingcompetitiveper- formance (59.04 vs. 60.93). For practical deployment, the decision should be based on the specific performance requirements of the application. 6. Conclusion ThispaperpresentsModalityCapabilityEnhancement(MCE),aprincipled framework that addresses imbalanced missing rates in incomplete multi-modal learning. The core innovation lies in the tightly coupled diagnosis–treatment loop: LCE dynamically identifies and incentivizes under-performing modalities throughadual-factormechanism,whileRCEtranslatestheseincentivesintoro- bust, cross-modally consistent features through subset prediction and auxiliary completion tasks. Theframework’sprincipalstrengthsarethreefold. First,itestablishesathe- oreticallygrounded approachtoimbalancemitigationthroughitsgame-theoretic formulation, providing rigorous quantification of modality contributions. Sec- ond, it maintains practical applicability through its dual-factor design. JSON: Name: mce_missing_modalities Title: Modality Capability Enhancement (MCE): a dual-factor incentive and representation framework for incomplete multi-modal learning with imbalanced missing rates Short Hypothesis: Jointly applying a dataset-level reweighting factor and a batch-level Shapley-derived learning-state incentive (LCE) together with subset prediction and cross-modal completion objectives (RCE) causes a statistically significant increase in average task performance across all modality subsets on imbalanced missing-rate multi-modal benchmarks, compared to (a) the same model without LCE, (b) the same model without RCE, or (c) existing baseline methods. Related Work: Existing approaches to incomplete multi-modal learning fall into reconstruction-based methods that impute missing modalities before fusion and analysis-based methods that extract shared or invariant features to avoid explicit reconstruction. Separate lines of work address modality imbalance by dataset-level reweighting or prototype/feature balancing. Prior sample-level valuation methods diagnose modality utility but either resample or impose costly procedures. Shapley-value techniques have been used mainly for post-hoc explanation or with simple utility functions and are not typically integrated into training as dynamic incentives. Limitations of prior methods include (1) reliance on random-missingness assumptions, (2) dataset-level corrections that ignore sample-level variation in modality utility, (3) lack of explicit mechanisms to repair degraded representations for frequently missing modalities, and (4) computational or methodological constraints that prevent simultaneous balancing of learning dynamics and representation quality. Abstract: This research addresses incomplete multi-modal learning when modalities have imbalanced missing rates. We propose Modality Capability Enhancement (MCE), a training framework that (1) applies Learning Capability Enhancement (LCE): a dataset-level reweighting factor to compensate unequal update frequency and a batch-level Shapley-derived incentive to detect per-sample modality under-utilization; and (2) applies Representation Capability Enhancement (RCE): multi-task supervision comprised of single-modality supervision, subset-based prediction, and auxiliary cross-modal feature completion. LCE diagnoses capability gaps and allocates learning incentives; RCE converts those incentives into task-relevant, interoperable representations. The combined loop is trained end-to-end and is fusion-operator agnostic. Expected outcomes are improved robustness to imbalanced missingness, recovery of minority-modal capability, and tighter, more discriminative feature spaces across modality subsets. The framework is designed to be evaluated on multiple benchmarks and to quantify the tradeoffs between Shapley computation accuracy and practical approximation. Experiments: Datasets: nuScenes (urban segmentation; use official train/val splits, BEV pre-processing), BraTS2020 (MRI tumor segmentation; 219 train / 50 val / 100 test, 4 MRI modalities, predict WT/TC/ET), IEMOCAP (emotion recognition; 4446/3899/3696 train/val/test utterances, acoustic/visual/lexical modalities, 4-class), AudiovisionMNIST (paired image/audio, 1500 pairs, 70/30 train/val). Baselines: backbone-only (fusion operator with no MCE), PMR, MBT-Sample, RedCore, PASSION, ShaSpec/ShaSpec-like, UniMF, SMIL, and single-modality upperbound models (frozen). Metrics: per-condition mean IoU (nuScenes), Dice scores WT/TC/ET (BraTS2020), classification accuracy and 95% CI (IEMOCAP, AudiovisionMNIST), representation metrics (intra-class distance, inter-class distance, intra/inter ratio, average intra-class cosine consistency), and compute metrics (FLOPs, GPU memory, forward/backward time). Experimental setup: for each dataset train with six imbalanced missing-rate configurations: permutations of (0.2,0.5,0.8) over modalities; report aggregated average across all non-empty modality subset test conditions. Architectures: EfficientNet+BEV pipeline for nuScenes; 3D U-Net encoders + mmFormer fusion for BraTS2020; LSTM/TextCNN encoders + FC decoder for IEMOCAP; LeNet5+audio MFCC encoder for AudiovisionMNIST. Optimizers and schedules per-dataset (AdamW or Adam, learning rates 1e-3 to 2e-4, batch sizes 1 for volumetric/BEV, 128 for IEMOCAP/MNIST). Repetition: run each configuration with 10 independent seeds; report mean ± std and paired statistical tests. Ablations: (1) baseline backbone; (2) RCE only: single supervision only, subset only, aux only, and their combinations; (3) LCE only: A-only (dataset-level), B-only (Shapley-only), and A+B; (4) full MCE (A+B + RCE); (5) Shapley calculation modes: exact (exhaustive for M≤6) vs Monte Carlo permutations with K∈{50,100,200} and measure approximation error vs runtime; (6) hyperparameter grid for λ_single, λ_sub, λ_aux with values {0.01,0.1,1,2,10} and report sensitivity. Additional evaluations: modality capability inspection by fixing encoders and training single-modality decoders to measure achievable upperbound vs learned capability; evaluate representation quality via clustering metrics; measure compute overhead (time, FLOPs, GPU memory) for each Shapley mode. Reporting: per-dataset tables of baselines vs ablations, statistical significance (p<0.05), and compute trade-offs. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Computational cost: exact Shapley computation scales exponentially with number of modalities and may be infeasible for M>6; Monte Carlo approximations add estimator variance and may degrade the B signal. 2) Dependence on reliable unimodal upperbounds: frozen single-modal models may be unavailable or poorly estimated, biasing U and therefore B. 3) Hyperparameter sensitivity: three auxiliary loss weights and scaling/normalization of A/B may require dataset-specific tuning; suboptimal settings can destabilize training. 4) Scalability: transformer-based reconstruction and subset supervision increase memory and time, limiting use on large-scale or high-resolution data. 5) Missing-all case: framework excludes samples with no observed modalities and does not address situations where all modalities are absent. 6) Generalization and distribution shift: MCE is evaluated on specific vision/medical/audio benchmarks and may not generalize to modalities with qualitatively different statistics or adversarial missingness mechanisms. 7) Evaluation bias: reported gains may depend on the chosen backbones, fusion operators, or dataset preprocessing; cross-architecture generality must be verified. 8) Privacy and data constraints: training frozen unimodal models or computing Shapley values over large batches may raise privacy or compliance concerns in certain domains.
